items.title: Frozen assets: the rise and fall of the ice trade

topic.th: ประวัติศาสตร์เศรษฐกิจ

paragraphs: Before the age of electricity, keeping anything cold in a hot climate was a luxury reserved for the very wealthy. Rulers in Persia, China and the Mediterranean had stored winter snow in pits and thick-walled buildings for centuries, but the quantities were small and the cold rarely travelled far. That changed in the nineteenth century, when an unlikely industry grew up around a resource that seemed, to most people, entirely worthless: the ice that formed each winter on the lakes and ponds of New England. Within a few decades, frozen water cut from those ponds was being sold in the Caribbean, in South America and as far away as India.

The industry is usually traced to Frederic Tudor, a young Boston merchant who in 1806 sent a ship loaded with ice to the Caribbean island of Martinique. His contemporaries thought the plan absurd, and the first voyages appeared to prove them right. Much of the cargo melted before it could be sold, and the islanders who received the rest had little idea what to do with it. Tudor's difficulty, however, was not the crossing itself; ice packed tightly in a ship's hold melts far more slowly than most people expected. The real problem lay at the destination, where there was nowhere to keep the ice once it had been unloaded. Only after years of heavy losses, including a spell in prison for debt, did he begin to build insulated ice houses in the ports he supplied.

Two developments turned this fragile business into a profitable one. The first was the choice of insulation. Early shippers had experimented with straw, hay and rice husks, but sawdust proved the most effective, and it had the additional merit of being almost free, since the timber mills of Maine produced it in enormous quantities as waste. The second was the mechanisation of harvesting. Cutting ice by hand with axes and saws produced blocks of uneven size that wasted space in storage and in transit. A horse-drawn cutter, introduced by one of Tudor's suppliers, Nathaniel Wyeth, scored the frozen surface of a pond in a regular grid, so that workers could split it into identical blocks that could be stacked with almost no gaps between them. Tightly stacked blocks melted more slowly, because less of their surface was exposed to warm air.

With these improvements, the trade expanded rapidly. In 1833 a cargo of ice left Boston for Calcutta, a voyage of around four months that took the ship twice across the equator; more than half of the ice was still frozen when it arrived. By the middle of the century, ships were carrying ice to ports throughout the tropics, and the ponds around Boston had become so valuable that the rights to harvest them were bought and sold like farmland. The writer Henry David Thoreau, who lived for two years beside Walden Pond, recorded watching a large team of labourers remove ice from its surface one winter, and reflected that the water he drank might one day cool a glass in India.

Yet the largest market for natural ice was never overseas. As cities in the United States grew, so did the demand for ice at home. Households bought it to fill wooden iceboxes, in which food could be kept fresh for several days, while brewers needed it to produce lager, a style of beer that must be fermented at low temperatures. Meat-packers in the Midwest packed ice into railway wagons to send fresh beef to the cities of the east coast, an innovation that changed the national diet. In Europe a similar pattern emerged, although most of the supply came not from America but from Norway, whose lakes provided ice that was shipped across the North Sea to British ports in huge quantities.

The success of the industry concealed two weaknesses. The first was its dependence on the weather. A mild winter could leave the ponds too thin to cut, and in such years the price of ice rose sharply; the shortages that followed were known as ice famines. The second weakness was purity. As towns grew along rivers and lakes, the water that froze into ice was increasingly polluted by sewage and industrial waste, and doctors began to warn that the same ice that preserved food could also spread disease. Public confidence, once lost, proved hard to restore.

These problems created an opening for a competitor. Machines that produced ice by compressing and expanding gases had existed since the middle of the century, but they had been expensive and unreliable. As the technology improved, factory-made ice, known in the trade as plant ice, became cheaper; made from filtered water, it could be produced in any season and in any town, close to the customers who needed it. The arrival of affordable electric refrigerators in private homes during the 1920s and 1930s removed the need for regular ice deliveries, and an industry that had once employed tens of thousands of people faded almost entirely from public memory.

items.title: Losing the dark

topic.th: มลพิษทางแสงและนิเวศวิทยา

paragraphs: For almost the whole history of life on Earth, night has been reliably dark. The brightness of the night sky varied with the phases of the moon and with the weather, but it never approached that of day, and the daily alternation between light and darkness became built into the bodies of nearly every living thing. In little more than a century, that pattern has been disrupted across much of the planet. Satellite images show continents outlined in light, and a widely cited atlas published in 2016 estimated that more than four-fifths of the world's population lives under skies measurably brightened by artificial lighting. In Europe and North America, almost nobody now lives beneath a truly natural night sky.

Measuring the change has proved surprisingly difficult. Satellites are the obvious tool, but most of those that photograph the Earth at night are poorly suited to the task. Some cannot detect the blue part of the spectrum, so they record the replacement of orange street lamps by white light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, as a fall in brightness even when the sky above a city is becoming brighter to the human eye. For this reason, some of the most revealing evidence has come from the ground. In a long-running project, thousands of volunteers around the world compared the night sky with a set of star charts, recording the faintest stars visible from where they stood. Analysed together, their observations between 2011 and 2022 suggested that the sky was growing brighter by nearly ten per cent a year, far faster than satellite measurements had indicated.

The consequences for wildlife are most dramatic among animals that use light to find their way. Sea turtles provide the classic example. Hatchlings emerge from nests on the beach at night and head instinctively towards the brightest part of the horizon, which, on an unlit coast, is the open sea reflecting the glow of the sky. Where hotels and roads line the shore, the young turtles may crawl inland instead, and die from exhaustion, predators or traffic. On some coasts, volunteers now patrol the beaches during the nesting season, asking residents to draw their curtains and switch off outdoor lights. Many migrating birds, which often travel at night, are drawn towards brightly lit buildings, particularly on cloudy nights when the stars are hidden, and may circle them until they collapse or collide with glass.

The attraction of insects to lamps has been noticed for as long as people have lit fires, yet its cause was poorly understood until recently. It was long suggested that moths steer by keeping the moon at a fixed angle and are confused by nearer lights. In 2024, however, researchers who filmed insects in flight with high-speed cameras proposed a simpler explanation. Flying insects appear to keep their backs turned towards the brightest part of their surroundings, which in nature is the sky. When the brightest point is a lamp to one side, this reflex tips them sideways or even upside down, and they circle helplessly around it. Whatever the mechanism, the scale of the effect is considerable: a single street light can draw in insects from a wide surrounding area, removing them from the food chains and pollination networks on which other species depend.

Humans are not immune. The body's internal clock is set chiefly by light received through the eyes, and exposure to light in the evening delays the release of melatonin, a hormone associated with the onset of sleep. Light at the blue end of the spectrum, which is abundant in many white LEDs and in the screens of phones, is especially effective at producing this delay. Night-shift workers, whose exposure to light after dark is greater than anyone else's, have been studied particularly closely. Studies have linked high levels of outdoor light at night with poorer sleep and with a range of health problems, although researchers acknowledge that people living in brightly lit areas differ from others in many ways, so that cause and effect are hard to separate.

Unlike many forms of pollution, light pollution can be reduced almost immediately and at modest cost. A large share of outdoor light shines sideways or upwards, where it illuminates nothing useful. Moreover, because light leaves no residue in soil or water, the benefits of any change begin the moment the lamps are adjusted. Shielded fittings that direct light only downwards, lamps that are dimmed or switched off late at night, and warmer colours containing less blue light can all reduce the problem without making streets less safe. A number of towns and protected areas have been recognised as dark-sky places after adopting such measures, and some report that the resulting views of the stars have attracted visitors.

The obstacle is less technical than psychological. Brightness is widely associated with security and prosperity, and residents often oppose reductions in street lighting even where there is little evidence that brighter lighting reduces crime. The switch to LEDs illustrates the difficulty. Because the new lamps are far cheaper to run, many authorities have installed more of them, or made them brighter, cancelling much of the expected environmental benefit. Campaigners for darker skies argue that the real task is not to persuade people to accept darkness, but to convince them that well-designed lighting, aimed where it is needed and used when it is needed, is better lighting rather than less.

items.title: Bringing back the dead: the case against de-extinction

topic.th: ชีววิทยาการอนุรักษ์และพันธุวิศวกรรม

paragraphs: In April 2025, a biotechnology company in the United States announced that it had produced three wolf pups which, it claimed, were the first dire wolves to walk the Earth for more than ten thousand years. The animals were in fact grey wolves whose DNA had been altered at a small number of sites to give them some of the physical features, such as a larger frame and a pale coat, that scientists associate with their extinct relative. The announcement attracted enormous attention, much of it admiring, and a predictable chorus of criticism. Both reactions, I want to suggest, missed the more interesting question. The issue is not whether such animals are really dire wolves, but what we hope to achieve by making them, and whether the same effort could achieve more elsewhere.

The term de-extinction promises more than any current technique can deliver. An extinct species cannot be recreated from fragments of ancient DNA; what can be produced is a living relative engineered to resemble it in selected respects. Even the one case in which an extinct animal was, briefly, brought back illustrates the limits. In 2003 a team of Spanish and French scientists cloned a Pyrenean ibex, a wild goat whose last known member had died three years earlier, using cells preserved from that individual. The attempt required dozens of embryos to be transferred to surrogate goats, and only one pregnancy went to full term. The newborn kid lived for only a few minutes, killed by a defect in its lungs. Cloning requires intact cells, and for the overwhelming majority of extinct species none exist.

Defenders of the field reply that resemblance is enough. What matters ecologically, they argue, is not an animal's ancestry but what it does: how it grazes, how it disperses seeds, how it shapes the land. If an elephant engineered to withstand the cold could trample shrubs and maintain open grassland in the Arctic, as mammoths are thought to have done, it would hardly matter whether we called it a mammoth. Some researchers even suggest that such grazing could slow the thawing of frozen ground, since trampled snow allows winter cold to reach deeper into the soil. This is a serious argument, and in principle I accept it. The difficulty is that it turns de-extinction from a question of identity into a question of ecology, and on ecological grounds the proposals look far less persuasive.

Consider what restoring an ecological role would actually require. A single animal, or even a few dozen, does nothing to a landscape; a functioning population of large herbivores would need to number in the thousands and to be sustained over many generations. Elephants breed slowly, with a pregnancy lasting nearly two years, and their engineered cousins would need habitat, protection and, almost certainly, decades of intensive management. Meanwhile, the ecosystems into which they would be released have not stood still since the mammoths vanished: the climate, the vegetation and the human presence have all changed. There is no guarantee that a role played ten thousand years ago can be filled today, or that filling it would be beneficial.

The second objection concerns cost, and here the argument becomes uncomfortable for the enthusiasts. Money spent on recreating lost species is money not spent on keeping existing ones alive, and conservation budgets are already small in relation to the scale of the losses they are meant to prevent. One widely discussed analysis, which estimated the cost of maintaining revived species in the wild, concluded that the same sums could protect several times as many species that are threatened but still survive. Supporters respond that the private investors who fund de-extinction would not otherwise give to conservation, so nothing is truly diverted. That may be so, but it overlooks a subtler risk: if the public comes to believe that extinction can be reversed, the sense of urgency that drives support for conservation may weaken.

This is sometimes called the moral hazard of de-extinction, and I regard it as the strongest argument against the more extravagant claims made on the field's behalf. Few people treat a valuable vase carelessly simply because a restorer could glue the pieces together; but a belief that a lost species can be brought back may well make its loss seem less final, and therefore less serious. Presenting engineered wolves as the return of an extinct predator, as the 2025 announcement did, is precisely the kind of framing that encourages this belief.

None of this means that the underlying technology is worthless. On the contrary, its most promising uses have little to do with extinct animals. The black-footed ferret, a North American predator that was once reduced to a few dozen individuals, suffers from very low genetic diversity, because every living ferret descends from a handful of survivors. In 2020 scientists produced a clone from cells that had been frozen in the 1980s, reintroducing genetic variation that had been missing from the population for decades. Techniques developed for de-extinction might similarly be used to give endangered species resistance to disease, or to help corals cope with warmer seas.

The fairest conclusion, then, is that de-extinction is misnamed rather than misguided. As a promise to undo the losses of the past, it is unconvincing and potentially harmful. As a set of tools for protecting the species that remain, it may prove genuinely valuable. The test of the field over the coming decades will be whether its leaders are willing to describe their work in the second, more modest sense, even though that description is far less likely to make headlines. Such modesty would cost the field some publicity, but it would earn something more durable: the trust of the conservationists whose cooperation it will ultimately need.
